title: Earthen vessels (2 Corinthians 4:7)

lines: A STONE THROWN INTO A CAVE.
cards: In the winter of 1946 to 1947, a young Bedouin shepherd threw a stone into a cave above the Dead Sea and heard something break.

Inside were tall clay jars, and inside the jars, rolled scrolls: some of the oldest copies of the Hebrew scriptures ever found. Plain pots, the kind any household had, had kept them safe for nearly two thousand years.
Paul never saw those jars. But writing to Corinth, he reached for the same picture to describe himself and every Christian: treasure, kept in clay.

teach.b: Just before today's verse, Paul has been talking about light: the God who said, let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts.
Then he says what holds that light: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency may be of the power of God, and not of us."
The Greek word for earthen means plain baked clay, the stuff of ordinary pots and cheap oil lamps.
Corinth made clay lamps by the thousand, and some scholars think Paul has a lamp in mind: a cheap clay shell with a flame inside. Why would God choose clay?

Paul answers in the same verse: so it's obvious where the power comes from. The Corinthians were impressed by polished speakers, and some of them found Paul unimpressive. His answer isn't to polish himself up.
It's to point at the cracks.

In the next lines he lists them: pressed on every side but not crushed, perplexed but not in despair, persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed. The clay takes the blows. The treasure stays.
Catholics hear something of their own teaching here.

teach.h: THE SACRAMENTS DON'T DEPEND ON THE PRIEST.
teach.b: The Church holds that the sacraments don't depend on the holiness of the priest who celebrates them: Christ acts in them, through the minister. The priest is clay.
So is every bishop, every parent teaching a child the sign of the cross, every tired volunteer. That's not an excuse for carelessness.

teach.h: WE HAVE THIS TREASURE IN EARTHEN VESSELS.
teach.b: It's a kind of relief: the treasure was never theirs to begin with.

how: Catholic teaching holds that the sacraments act by the power of Christ, not by the worthiness of the minister (ex opere operato), which is often explained with this verse in mind.

o: fine pottery made for temple worship
plain clay jars that hold a treasure
ancient urns that hold the ashes of the dead

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: Paul answers his critics by showing how impressive he is
he points at his weakness, so the power is clearly God's.
in Catholic teaching a sacrament fails if the priest is unholy
the Church teaches Christ acts in the sacraments, whatever the minister's holiness.
the Greek for earthen means ordinary baked clay
the stuff of cheap pots and oil lamps.

games.q: your critics in Corinth say you're unimpressive and your speech is weak. how do you answer them?
o: hire a better speaker to read your letters.
admit you're clay, and say the power is God's.
games.why: "we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency may be of the power of God, and not of us."

practice: Pick up a mug or a ceramic bowl, or cup your empty hands as if holding one, and feel its weight, the rough base, maybe a chip on the rim you've stopped noticing.

Hold it gently, the way you'd hold something that could break, and think of yourself the same way: breakable, and carrying something. If you pray, thank God for what you carry; if not, notice how carefully you're holding it.

wordCard.voice: Earthen vessels. Paul's picture of himself and every Christian: plain clay jars, carrying a treasure that isn't their own. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: made of baked clay. from ostrakon, a potsherd, the same root as English 'ostracize'.

carryVoice: Your line: treasure in clay. Plain jars kept the scrolls safe. That's day five hundred seventy-seven.

sources.q: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency may be of the power of God, and not of us.
